tip.title: Verbs with me
tip.body: Many routine verbs come with a little extra pronoun: se lever (to get up) → je me lève, literally "I get myself up". Before a vowel me becomes m': je m'habille (I get dressed). In lève, the è is open like the e in "bed"; the final -e is silent.

tip.title: faire for chores
tip.body: Most household chores use faire: faire le ménage (do the cleaning), faire la vaisselle (do the dishes), faire la lessive (do the laundry), faire les courses (do the shopping). Vacuuming is passer l'aspirateur. In faire, the ai of je fais sounds like the è in lève.

lessons.title: Reflexive verbs
lessons.goal: Use me, te, se, nous, vous with routine verbs.

tip.title: The pronoun matches the subject
tip.body: Reflexive verbs take a pronoun that matches the subject: je me lève, tu te lèves, il / elle / on se lève, nous nous levons, vous vous levez, ils / elles se lèvent. me, te, se become m', t', s' before a vowel or silent h: je m'habille, il s'habille. Liaison: in nous nous_habillons and vous vous_habillez, the s before the vowel sounds like z. In the negative, ne… pas wraps around pronoun + verb: je ne me lève pas. With aller + infinitive, the pronoun goes with the infinitive and still matches: je vais me coucher, tu vas te coucher.

culture.title: La pause déjeuner
culture.body: In France the legal working week is 35 hours, and lunch is still a real break for many people: often a sit-down meal around noon or 1 pm, in a canteen, a café or with colleagues, and many employees get meal vouchers (tickets-restaurant). In smaller towns some shops close for lunch. In Switzerland lunch tends to be a little earlier, around noon. In Belgium, Switzerland and Québec this midday meal is le dîner — in Québec it is often quicker, sometimes eaten at the desk.
